opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on what you mean by "overtaking," and I'd separate it into a few dimensions.

The first is volume. If you just ask who's issuing more queries to the web, agents are on a trajectory to pass humans fairly soon, if they haven't already in some pockets. A single agent working on a task might fire off dozens or hundreds of searches where a person would do two or three. So in raw usage, the crossover is close, and I think it'll happen faster than most people expect.

The second dimension is quality: can an agent actually do the research task as well as a skilled human would? There, the way I think about it is to look at hard, realistic tasks, the kind where a diligent analyst would spend an hour or a day pulling information from many sources, reconciling conflicts, and checking facts. On simple lookups, agents are already better and much faster. On deep, multi-hop research, they're getting close to, and on some benchmarks exceeding, what a typical person achieves in a reasonable amount of time. But they still fall short of an expert who really knows where to look and what to trust.

The third dimension, and the one I care about most, is whether the web itself is built for them. Today's web, and today's search, were designed for humans: ten blue links, pages optimized for eyeballs and ads, interfaces that assume someone's going to click and scroll. Agents are working through infrastructure that wasn't made for them. So a big part of the gap isn't model intelligence. It's tooling. When you give agents search and retrieval built for how they actually consume information, meaning dense, verifiable, token-efficient, with provenance attached, their performance jumps significantly.

So my assessment is that on volume, the crossover is basically here. On capability for most practical tasks, we're within reach. And the thing that will really decide how quickly agents surpass humans is whether we build a web for agents rather than forcing them to use one built for us. That's the bet we're making.

r001.rationale: The response discusses agents issuing web searches and query volume, but does not explain that AI web-page-read traffic also includes crawler activity beyond searches.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the framing of "overtaking" is already a little off, because it assumes agents and humans are doing the same activity, and they're really not. When a person searches, they type two or three words, scan ten blue links, click one, maybe refine the query. That whole interface was designed around human attention and human patience. An agent doesn't have either constraint. It will happily issue fifty queries, read two hundred pages, cross-reference them, and never get bored. So on pure volume, I'd say agents aren't close to overtaking humans, they've already done it on a lot of the infrastructure we see. The majority of fetches hitting a lot of sites now are not a person on a browser.

Where it gets more interesting is quality, and I'd break that into a few pieces. One is retrieval: can the agent actually find the right page? I think we're mostly there for the easy stuff. Where it still breaks is the long tail, where the answer lives in a forum thread from 2014 or a PDF that was never really indexed well, and the agent confidently stops early because it found something plausible.

The second piece is judgment about sources, and this is where humans still have an edge that's underappreciated. A person has context: they know this blog is reliable, that outlet has an agenda, this result is SEO spam. Agents are getting better at this, but a lot of the web was built to game ranking systems, and now it's going to be built to game agents. That's an adversarial problem, not just a capability problem, and it won't be solved by a bigger model alone.

And the third piece is the one I spend the most time on, which is that the search stack itself was built for the wrong customer. The index, the ranking, the latency budget, the result format, all of it assumes a human is on the other end. When the caller is a model, you want a different contract: raw content rather than snippets, structured provenance, freshness guarantees, the ability to ask for depth rather than breadth. So my honest assessment is that agents are already ahead in throughput, roughly at parity on common tasks, still behind on taste and verification, and the real bottleneck isn't the agents, it's that we haven't rebuilt the search layer for them yet. That gap closes fast once the tooling catches up, and I think that's a matter of a couple of years, not a decade.

r001.rationale: The response says many site fetches are not from people using browsers, but it does not identify crawler activity or explain that AI page reads extend beyond web searches.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by overtaking humans. If you mean agents doing more of the searching on our behalf, that seems much closer than agents reliably handling every task we might give them. One user request can lead an agent to run several searches, compare results, and come back with an answer. So the volume of agent searches could grow very quickly.

The harder question is whether you can trust the agent to find the right information, recognize when sources disagree, and know when it hasn’t found enough. I’d distinguish between agents generating more searches and agents being consistently better at getting us what we need. Those are different milestones.

r001.rationale: The response discusses agents running searches and growing search volume, but it does not explain that AI web-page-read traffic also includes crawler activity beyond searches.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what we mean by overtaking humans. If you mean agents performing more searches than people do directly, that could happen well before agents can reliably handle every task people bring to the web. A single user request might cause an agent to run many searches, compare results, and follow up on missing information.

The harder question is whether you can trust the agent to find the right information and know when it has enough evidence. Search is part of that, but so are judging sources, resolving conflicting claims, and recognizing uncertainty. So I’d distinguish growth in search volume from the ability to complete useful work reliably. The latter is the more meaningful milestone.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes agent search volume from reliable task completion, but does not explain that AI web-page-read traffic includes crawler activity beyond web searches.
